# Self study - Session 1 {#sec-act1-selfstudy1}

This class contains self-study sessions to reinforce your understanding of the material and explore other aspects of the topic in a self-guided manner.

In this specific session, we will get hands-on with some essential tools for reporting: `uv`, `JupyterLab`, `seaborn`/`plotly`, and `Quarto`.

Each exercise focuses on a single topic.

The data set we will rely on in this session is a synthetic time series that simulates weekly production data of a manufacturing plant over 20 years.

First, download the data set from [here](../data/assets/act1/selfstudysessions/sss1_production_data.csv).

The data has three columns: `Date`, `pieces` and `pieces_gaps`. The column `pieces` contains the full data set without gaps, while `pieces_gaps` contains the same data set with several missing values (NaNs).
The period covered by the data set is from 2005-01-01 to 2024-12-31 in weekly frequency.

## Exercise A: `uv` — Environment Management

::: {.callout-caution appearance="simple" collapse="true" icon=false}
::::{#exr-basics-mv-space}
## Setting up an isolated environment with `uv`
::::

[`uv`](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) is a fast, modern package and environment manager.
It installs and manages Python versions and packages in isolated environments (`venv`).


1. Install `uv` following the [official instructions](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/).
2. In the project directory, initialize a new project and create a virtual environment using `uv`.
3. Install the following packages into the environment: `numpy`, `matplotlib`.
4. Verify the environment works by creating a simple Python script that creates a simple plot of $f(t) = (16 (\sin(t))^3, 13 \cos(t) - 5 \cos(2t) - 2 \cos(3t) - \cos(4t))$ using the `numpy` and `matplotlib` package. (Hint: Use `numpy.linspace` to create a range of values for `t`, the function produces the $x$ and $y$ coordinates of the plot.)

After this exercise you should be able to
1. Create and manage isolated Python environments using `uv`.
2. Install and manage Python packages within these environments.
3. Additionally be able to explain what `uv` does and why it is useful.
:::

Now that you have a working environment, you can use it to install additional packages as needed for the exercises below.

::: {.callout-caution appearance="simple" collapse="true" icon=false}
::::{#exr-basics-mv-space}
## Working with JupyterLab
::::

[JupyterLab](https://jupyterlab.readthedocs.io/en/stable/getting_started/overview.html) is a web-based interactive development environment (IDE) for Jupyter Notebooks. It provides a flexible interface for interactive data exploration and reporting.

1. Launch JupyterLab from your `uv` environment by adding it to your environment first or alternatively, using VS Code, you can also use the Jupyter extension instead.
2. Create a new notebook called `production_explore.ipynb`.
3. Load the production data set (the CSV with `Date`, `pieces`, `pieces_gaps`) into a `pandas` DataFrame using a code cell.
4. Display the first 10 rows and print basic statistics.
5. Create a line plot of `pieces` over time using `matplotlib`.
6. Experiment with different cell types: code, markdown, and raw cells.
7. Export the notebook as HTML and PDF.

After this exercise you should be able to:

1. Create and organize notebooks in JupyterLab.
2. Differentiate between code, markdown, and raw cells.
3. Export notebooks to other formats (HTML, PDF).
4. Structure a notebook with self-contained, readable code cells.
:::


`matplotlib` is a widely used Python library for creating static visualizations.
`seaborn` is a statistical data visualization library built on top of `matplotlib`, providing a high-level interface for drawing attractive and informative statistical graphics and 
`plotly` is an interactive data visualization library that allows you to create dynamic, web-based visualizations.

::: {.callout-caution appearance="simple" collapse="true" icon=false}
:::{#exr-basics-mv-space}
## Visualizing the production data
:::

In this exercise you will visualize the production data using both `seaborn` (static, statistical plots) and `plotly` (interactive plots).

**Using seaborn:**
1. Load the production data set and use `seaborn` to create:
   - A line plot of `pieces` over time.
   - A pair plot of the numeric columns.
   - A box plot of `pieces` by year (extract the year from the `Date` column).
2. Observe patterns and note any anomalies visually.

**Using plotly:**
3. Recreate the line plot of `pieces` using `plotly` as an interactive figure.
4. Use the provided `plot_production_data` function to visualize both `pieces` and `pieces_gaps` together.

After this exercise you should be able to:

1. Create basic static statistical plots with `seaborn`.
2. Create basic interactive plots with `plotly`.
3. Explore the interactive features of `plotly`: zoom in on specific time periods, hover over data points to see exact values.
4. Compare and discuss the strengths and weaknesses of each library.
:::


Congratulations, you are now able to create and manage isolated Python environments, work with JupyterLab, and visualize data using both static and interactive plotting libraries.
The next step is to integrate your code and visualizations into a comprehensive report which you can hand over to stakeholders using Quarto.

::: {.callout-caution appearance="simple" collapse="true" icon=false}
::::{#exr-basics-mv-space}
## Generating a report with Quarto
::::

[Quarto](https://quarto.org/) is an open-source scientific and technical publishing system.
It allows you to create dynamic documents, reports, and presentations from your code and narrative text.
The material of this course itself is rendered using Quarto.

1. Create a Quarto Markdown (`.qmd`) file in your project.
2. Embed the code and plots from the previous two exercises into the Quarto document.
3. Use code chunk options to control output (e.g., `echo=FALSE` to hide code, `fig-width` to set figure dimensions).
4. Render the document as HTML and PDF.
5. Explore collapsing code chunks in your document (see [Quarto docs](https://quarto.org/docs/jupyter/authoring.html#code-chunk-options)).

After this exercise you should be able to:

1. Create a Quarto document that integrates code, output, and narrative.
2. Render Quarto documents to HTML and PDF formats.
:::
